p.x:
Nina is a reporter for a local newspaper in Phuket. Every morning, she reads other newspapers and listens to the radio to find stories. Then she goes to the office for a meeting with the other reporters. They decide which stories are important for today.
Yesterday, Nina wrote a report about a new beach clean-up programme. She interviewed the organisers and some tourists. In her article, she wrote only the facts, not her opinion. "A good reporter must always tell the truth," she says. "Readers need to know that what they read is true."
Her story was on the front page, with the headline "Tourists Help Clean Phuket's Beaches". Later, a TV station called her, and she appeared on a news show to talk about it. Next month, a magazine wants her to write an article about local food.

Every day, we are surrounded by information from the media: newspapers, TV, websites and social media. But how do we know what is true?
Professional journalists follow rules. Before an editor allows a story to be published, the journalist usually checks it with at least two sources. On TV, presenters read news that has been checked by a team. Documentaries can take months or even years to research.
Social media is different. Anyone can post anything, and a rumour can reach millions of viewers before anyone checks it. Gossip about a celebrity's private life often spreads faster than important news about the economy. Some stories are simple mistakes; others are a deliberate lie.
So what can we do? Experts suggest asking three questions: Who wrote this? What is their source? Has anyone else reported it? When a story makes you very angry or very excited, be especially careful. A trustworthy news organisation will also broadcast corrections when it gets something wrong.

p.t: News in the Age of the Algorithm
p.x:
For most of the twentieth century, a few newspapers and TV channels decided what counted as news. Foreign correspondents reported from around the world, and editors chose which stories received front-page coverage. Critics complained of bias, but most people at least shared the same basic facts.
Today, the situation is very different. Online platforms reward stories that attract clicks, encouraging sensational headlines and clickbait. Tabloid-style scandals about celebrities often receive more attention than serious reporting. Meanwhile, in some countries, governments use censorship to block independent news and spread propaganda instead.
This makes it harder for audiences to know which sources are credible. Some argue that truly objective journalism has always been impossible, since every reporter makes choices about what to include. Others insist that professional standards, such as checking facts and correcting errors, still make a crucial difference.
Ultimately, media literacy may be the most important skill of the twenty-first century: the ability to question what we read, recognise bias and seek out a range of perspectives.
